## Why angle/2?
You need an axis and an angle to rotate in 3D. But why do quaternions use a mysterious angle/2:

$$q = \cos(\theta/2) + \hat{\text{axis}}*\sin(\theta/2)$$

It becomes clear if you think of a quaternion as a reflection in two planes going through the origin

<div class="lab-mount lab-short" data-lab="planes" data-theta="60"></div>

## Why translation/2?
The mysterious "half" also pops up with translations too 

$$ \text{Dual Quaternion Translator} = 1 - \frac{\Delta x}{2} e_{01} - \frac{\Delta y}{2} e_{02} - \frac{\Delta z}{2} e_{03} $$

Makes sense if you think of it as a reflection across two parallel planes

<div class="lab-mount lab-short" data-lab="parallel" data-d="0.5"></div>

## How to use dual quaternions?
Combine a rotation $R$ then a translation $T$ by multipying them in the correct order:

$$TR$$  

Rotate then translate a point $P$ by using the sandwich:

$$TR(P)(TR)^{-1}$$

But how to multiply these things?


## Let's play DQ Candy Crush!
Use the rules: 
$$e_1^2 = e_2^2 = e_3^2 = 1$$ 

$$e_0^2 = 0$$

You can swap the order of multiplication by flipping the sign.

<div class="lab-mount" data-lab="blades" data-indices="012123"></div>
